cards.front: At both 2 and 4 months a child receives the hexavalent DTPa-hepB-IPV-Hib, pneumococcal conjugate, and oral [___].
cards.context:
The 2- and 4-month visits are identical in content, which makes them easy to hold together.

Each gives the hexavalent combination (DTPa-hepB-IPV-Hib), pneumococcal conjugate, and a dose of oral rotavirus.

cards.front: Amoxicillin cannot clear Bordetella pertussis from the airway epithelium — eradication needs the [___] antibiotic class.
cards.context:
The organism sits ON the ciliated epithelium and drives disease through secreted toxins, so the drug must reach and clear surface carriage — a job beta-lactams fail at.

Treating is mostly about interrupting spread to vulnerable contacts, especially unimmunised infants. Started in the paroxysmal phase, it barely changes the patient's own cough.

cards.front: A weak boy has enlarged firm calves because fat and fibrous tissue have replaced the muscle. That calf finding is [___].
cards.context: Calf pseudohypertrophy is enlargement from fat and fibrous tissue replacing muscle. In a weak boy it suggests Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

cards.front: Infant respiratory vulnerability: smaller airways (resistance ∝ 1/radius⁴), compliant chest walls, fewer alveoli, fetal [___] until 6 months.
cards.context:
Resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius — halve the diameter, sixteen-fold the resistance. So even small amounts of mucosal oedema in an infant airway dramatically increase work of breathing.

Compliant chest walls don't generate negative pressure efficiently, fewer alveoli mean less reserve, and fetal Hb's high O2 affinity slows release at the tissue level.

cards.front: A reduced FEV1/FVC ratio with a scooped expiratory limb is the [___] spirometry pattern.
cards.context: Obstruction lowers FEV1/FVC while FVC stays relatively preserved. The matching loop scoops on expiration as small airways collapse with falling lung volume.

cards.front: Pertussis (whooping cough) is treated with [___] (first-line macrolide).
cards.context:
Bordetella pertussis attaches to ciliated respiratory epithelium and acts mostly via toxins released at the cell surface — by the time paroxysmal cough appears the antibiotic does little for the patient.

Azithromycin is preferred — better tolerated than erythromycin, simplest paediatric regimen (5 days), and reduces transmission even when started late.

cards.front: Croup is caused by parainfluenza virus; peak age ~2 years; classic triad of barking cough, hoarse voice, [___].
cards.context:
Parainfluenza causes ~75% of croup; RSV, adenovirus, influenza, and rhinovirus account for the rest.

Symptoms classically worsen overnight from supine position and increased oedema.

cards.front: Itchy, transient, raised wheals that each individually resolve within 24 hours are [___].
cards.context: Urticaria is mast-cell-driven dermal oedema. Acute cases are usually post-viral or allergic and respond to non-sedating antihistamines; individual wheals lasting over 24 hours suggest urticarial vasculitis.

cards.front: On digital rectal exam in Hirschsprung disease the rectum is characteristically [___], and withdrawal of the finger may release an explosive gush of stool and gas.
cards.context:
Stool cannot pass the tonically contracted aganglionic segment, so it accumulates proximally. The examining finger briefly opens that narrow segment, releasing pent-up stool and gas — the 'blast sign'.

Functional constipation gives the opposite picture: a capacious rectum loaded with stool.

cards.front: Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in a boy aged 4–10 is [___].
cards.context: Hip pain by age is the highest-yield paediatric ortho pattern. Avascular necrosis of the femoral head strikes the 4–10 boy; younger onset means more remodelling time and a better prognosis.

cards.front: Pyloric stenosis: onset age 2-8 weeks; projectile non-bilious vomiting + hungry after; bloods show hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic [___].
cards.context:
Pyloric stenosis: hypertrophic pyloric muscle obstructs gastric outflow, onset 2-8 weeks. Triad: projectile non-bilious vomiting, HUNGRY after (distinguishes from gastro), palpable 'olive' epigastric mass.

Bloods: hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (HCl loss). Treat with rehydration + Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.

cards.front: Paediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT) components: Appearance, Work of Breathing, and [___] to skin.
cards.context:
PAT is a 60-second visual triage from across the room before touching the child.

Trust the gestalt. A floppy quiet infant 'who doesn't look right' may have sepsis hours before obs become abnormal.

cards.front: Intermittent colicky pain with drawing up of the legs, vomiting, and later redcurrant-jelly stool in an infant suggests [___].
cards.context:
Peak age is 3-18 months, classically after a viral illness enlarges Peyer's patches to form the ileocolic lead point. Between episodes the child may look deceptively well.

Redcurrant-jelly stool is a late, ischaemic sign — do not wait for it; ultrasound shows the target sign.

cards.front: A guideline's antibiotic duration usually counts the [___] IV-plus-oral course rather than a new course after step-down.
cards.context:
RCH durations generally mean the minimum total treatment, combining intravenous and oral days. Switching route does not reset the course clock.

Duration still changes with source control, organism, complications and response, so use a site-specific guideline rather than extending treatment by habit.

cards.front: Crohn's disease affects mouth to [___] with skip lesions and transmural inflammation; small bowel Crohn's may present insidiously with growth failure.
cards.context:
Crohn's disease can affect anywhere from mouth to anus, with skip lesions (unaffected bowel between affected segments) and transmural inflammation that drives fistulas, strictures, and abscesses.

Small bowel Crohn's is insidious — vague abdominal pain, intermittent loose stool, growth failure, low-grade fevers — easily missed for months.

cards.front: Intussusception is most common from 3 months to 2 years, peaking at 4-9 months; classic findings include a 'sausage-shaped' RUQ mass and 'redcurrant jelly' stool (late sign of [___]).
cards.context:
Intussusception (bowel telescoping into an adjacent segment) is most common from 3 months to 2 years, peaking at 4-9 months.

Most ileocolic, no lead point. USS shows target sign. First-line: pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction; surgery if failed or unstable.

cards.front: CGD: defective neutrophil [___] burst; recurrent bacterial and fungal infections; granuloma formation; diagnose with DHR test.
cards.context:
Chronic granulomatous disease: defective NADPH oxidase means neutrophils can phagocytose but can't kill catalase-positive organisms (Staph aureus, Burkholderia, Aspergillus, Nocardia, Serratia).

Diagnosis: dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry (DHR test).

Treatment: lifelong prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole + itraconazole; HSCT for cure.

cards.front: In craniosynostosis a skull suture fuses early, and the skull then grows [___] to the fused suture, giving the characteristic head shape.
cards.context:
A fused suture blocks growth across it, so the skull compensates by growing parallel to it; this predicts the head shape.

With multiple fused sutures, the vault cannot expand with the brain, raising intracranial pressure.

cards.front: Viral-induced wheeze is common in first [___] years; rhinovirus is the dominant trigger in school-aged children.
cards.context:
Respiratory viruses commonly trigger wheeze in young children, who may be well between episodes.

Episodic viral and multi-trigger labels are unreliable preschool subtypes; assess symptoms, episode burden and treatment response over time. Rhinovirus also triggers asthma exacerbations in school-aged children.

Atopy and recurrent wheeze increase concern for persistent asthma, but an infection-only pattern does not exclude it.

cards.front: CMV is the most common congenital infection causing sensorineural hearing loss; can be progressive or late-onset, so needs [___] audiological follow-up.
cards.context:
Congenital CMV is the commonest non-genetic cause of congenital sensorineural hearing loss — accounts for ~20% of paediatric hearing loss.

Any child with congenital CMV needs serial audiological follow-up through early childhood, even if initial UNHS normal.

cards.front: In a child with significant paracetamol overdose, the major target organ for toxicity is the [___].
cards.context: Excess toxic metabolite can overwhelm glutathione defences. Acetylcysteine treatment is time sensitive; early absence of symptoms does not exclude later injury.

cards.front: Oligoarticular JIA is commonly positive for [___] and requires screening for silent anterior uveitis.
cards.context: ANA does not diagnose JIA. Oligoarticular disease is commonly ANA-positive and carries a risk of silent anterior uveitis, so affected children need slit-lamp surveillance.

cards.front: A band of hair loss over the occiput in a thriving 3-month-old is caused by friction from lying [___].
cards.context:
Recognising this as benign avoids an unnecessary work-up. It appears around 2-3 months and regrows without treatment.

It is a friction effect of safe-sleep positioning, not a sign of neglect or nutritional deficiency.

cards.front: The structured psychosocial screening framework for an adolescent interview is the [___] assessment.
cards.context: The structured way to take an adolescent psychosocial history, moving from least to most sensitive: Home, Education/Employment, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/depression, Safety.

reference.title: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

cards.front: Swelling pushing the pinna down and forward after acute otitis media (AOM) indicates acute [___].
cards.context:
The mastoid air cells communicate with the middle ear, so unresolved acute otitis media can erode posteriorly into the mastoid bone.

This is a surgical emergency: IV third-generation cephalosporin, ENT review, and usually grommet ± cortical mastoidectomy.

cards.front: In cystic fibrosis, obstruction of small airways by viscous secretions causes bronchial wall damage and [___], typically worst in the upper lobes.
cards.context:
The structural lung damage of cystic fibrosis has a lobar preference worth knowing.

Viscous secretions obstruct small airways, causing distal atelectasis and progressive bronchial wall damage. The resulting bronchiectasis is typically worst in the upper lobes.

cards.front: Children with HbSS develop functional asplenia by age 5 → susceptibility to [___] organisms; need penicillin prophylaxis + pneumococcal/meningococcal vaccination.
cards.context:
Repeated splenic infarction from sickling causes functional asplenia by age 5 in HbSS — the spleen is shrunken, fibrotic, and non-functional.

Penicillin prophylaxis from diagnosis (often lifelong), pneumococcal + meningococcal vaccination.

cards.front: Paediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT) components: [___], Work of Breathing, and Circulation to skin.
cards.context:
PAT is a 60-second visual triage from across the room before touching the child.

Trust the gestalt. A floppy quiet infant 'who doesn't look right' may have sepsis hours before obs become abnormal.

cards.front: Breath-holding spells begin in infancy (peak 12-18 months) and typically resolve by age [___] years; trigger → crying → expiratory breath-hold → loss of awareness; benign but check ECG and treat any iron deficiency.
cards.context:
Breath-holding spells affect 6 months-6 years (peak 12-18 months, usually resolved by age 6).

Trigger (fear, pain, frustration) → crying → expiratory breath-hold → cyanosis or pallor → stiffening, loss of awareness, sometimes clonic jerks.

Two types: cyanotic (commonest, after crying) and pallid (after pain/fright, vasovagal) — benign, no long-term effects. Iron deficiency association — correction may help; always check ECG to rule out arrhythmia.

cards.front: Osmotic diarrhoea [___] on fasting; secretory diarrhoea persists on fasting.
cards.context:
The fasting test is the bedside discriminator.

Osmotic diarrhoea is driven by unabsorbed solutes (lactose in lactase deficiency, sorbitol from chewing gum) drawing water into the lumen — remove the trigger and diarrhoea stops within 24-48 h.

cards.front: An obese 10-year-old still snores with witnessed apnoeas after adenotonsillectomy. Treat this as residual OSA and reassess severity with [___] rather than assuming surgery cured it.
cards.context:
Adenotonsillectomy treats the common adenotonsillar obstruction but is not a cure guarantee. Obesity, severe baseline OSA and craniofacial, genetic or neuromuscular comorbidity make residual disease more likely.

Ongoing snoring or witnessed pauses after surgery should trigger objective reassessment with polysomnography rather than another recall of the original first-line rule.

A sleep or ENT team then targets any remaining obstruction; CPAP is an option when clinically significant OSA persists without a suitable site-specific treatment.

cards.front: The most common site for an ectopic testis is the [___] inguinal pouch.
cards.context: Ectopic testis has left the normal descent line. Commonest ectopic site: superficial inguinal pouch (external oblique aponeurosis ↔ Scarpa's fascia).

cards.front: Bordetella pertussis is a Gram-[___] aerobic coccobacillus; mortality is ~1 in 125 babies under 6 months.
cards.context:
Bordetella pertussis is a Gram-negative aerobic coccobacillus — it colonises ciliated respiratory epithelium and acts via secreted toxins (it is not an intracellular pathogen).

Azithromycin is given to eradicate the organism and limit spread, not because the bacterium hides inside cells. Infant mortality reflects apnoea and pulmonary hypertension from severe paroxysmal coughing.

Maternal vaccination in pregnancy + cocoon strategy is the main protection for infants too young for their own vaccine.

cards.front: Empirical antibiotics for suspected early-onset neonatal sepsis are benzylpenicillin plus [___].
cards.context:
Early-onset neonatal sepsis is covered for group B streptococcus, E. coli and listeria: benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin. Gentamicin needs levels because the neonatal kidney clears it slowly.

If meningitis is possible, cefotaxime replaces or joins gentamicin, because gentamicin does not enter the CSF.

cards.front: Lower limit of systolic BP in children 1-10 years = [___] + (2 × age); below this is hypotension and signals late-stage decompensated shock.
cards.context:
70 + (2 × age) gives the lower SBP limit in children 1-10 — a 5-year-old's floor is 80 mmHg. Useful in resus when age-specific tables aren't to hand.

The trap: children compensate via tachycardia and vasoconstriction up to ~30-40% volume loss, then crash. Hypotension means late Class III-IV shock (peri-arrest).

Treat tachycardia, cold peripheries, prolonged cap refill, oliguria, or altered mental status as compensated shock — don't wait for the BP to drop.

cards.front: A blanching maculopapular rash spreading down from behind the ears, with high fever and the 3 Cs (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), is [___].
cards.context:
Measles is highly infectious and notifiable — isolate the child. Koplik spots precede the rash by 1-2 days.

Watch for otitis media, pneumonia, encephalitis, and late SSPE.

cards.front: A child develops ear pain after swimming. Pulling the outer ear is painful; pressing the [___] also reproduces pain. These findings support otitis externa.
cards.context: Inflammation of the external canal makes manipulation painful. Pinna traction is usually better tolerated in uncomplicated middle-ear infection.

cards.front: A seven-year-old has a persistent limp and knee pain despite a normal knee examination. Hip rotation is restricted and radiographs show femoral-head fragmentation. The likely diagnosis is [___].
cards.context:
Loss of blood supply weakens the growing femoral head, which can fragment or collapse before repair. The hip can refer pain to the thigh or knee.

A normal knee examination should therefore lead you to examine the hip, including internal rotation and abduction.

cards.front: The five CRASH features of Kawasaki disease are conjunctivitis, rash, [___], strawberry tongue and hand and foot changes.
cards.context:
CRASH is the retrieval handle: Conjunctivitis, Rash, Adenopathy, Strawberry tongue, Hands and feet. Fever is required on top of these, not one of them.

The features accumulate rather than appearing together, so a child seen early can look incomplete and still have the disease.

Conjunctivitis is bilateral and non-purulent, and the node qualifies at 1.5 cm or more, usually on one side.

cards.front: Croup is caused by parainfluenza virus; peak age ~[___] years; classic triad of barking cough, hoarse voice, stridor.
cards.context:
Parainfluenza causes ~75% of croup; RSV, adenovirus, influenza, and rhinovirus account for the rest.

Symptoms classically worsen overnight from supine position and increased oedema.

cards.front: The lacy, net-like mottling of a cold but otherwise well infant that fades on warming is cutis [___].
cards.context:
Cutis marmorata is a physiological vasomotor response to cold — symmetrical, reticulated, and it disappears with warming.

The trap is fixed mottling: mottling that persists in a warm infant is a perfusion sign and belongs in the sepsis workup, not the reassurance pile.

cards.front: Community-governed primary care for First Nations families is delivered through the services abbreviated [___].
cards.context:
Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Services are governed by the communities they serve.

Referral into ACCHS pathways, and involving the Aboriginal Liaison Officer while the family is still in the department, materially changes follow-up rates. Do it during the admission, not in the discharge letter.

cards.front: An unimmunised 3-year-old has fever, drooling, soft stridor and sits forward in a tripod posture. Before any bloods or throat examination, the definitive step is [___] in theatre with ENT present.
cards.context:
Drooling, stridor and the tripod posture in a febrile toxic child is epiglottitis until proven otherwise, and the throat is not examined because provoking the child can occlude the airway.

The child stays with the parent, upright, while senior anaesthetics and ENT are called. The airway is secured by intubation in theatre with surgical backup, then cultures and ceftriaxone.

cards.front: Primary haemostasis (platelet plug, mucocutaneous bleeding) is mediated by [___] and vWF; secondary haemostasis (deep bleeding) is mediated by coagulation factors.
cards.context:
Primary haemostasis: platelets + vWF form the initial platelet plug at sites of vascular injury.

Secondary haemostasis: coagulation factor cascade generates fibrin thrombus stabilising the clot.

Defects cause deep bleeding (joints, muscles, post-surgical) — haemophilia A/B, factor deficiencies, anticoagulation.

cards.front: The worst-prognosis Salter-Harris injury is a [___] of the physis (type V), often invisible on the initial X-ray.
cards.context:
A crush injury of the physis leaves no displaced fragment, so the first X-ray often looks normal and the diagnosis is only made later when growth arrest appears.

That occult nature, plus full-thickness damage to the germinal layer, is why type V carries the worst prognosis.

cards.front: Hirschsprung disease: absence of [___] cells in distal bowel; most commonly rectosigmoid (short-segment, 80%); diagnose with suction rectal biopsy.
cards.context:
Hirschsprung is congenital absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus of distal bowel — the failure of neural crest cell migration during embryogenesis.

Short-segment (rectosigmoid only) is commonest at 80%; long-segment and total colonic less common but more severe.

Diagnosis: suction rectal biopsy (gold standard) showing absent ganglion cells + hypertrophied nerves.

cards.front: [___] introduction of allergenic foods (peanut, egg) via oral route promotes tolerance before transcutaneous sensitisation; supported by LEAP and EAT studies.
cards.context:
The skin barrier hypothesis: cutaneous (eczema-mediated) exposure primes Th2 sensitisation; oral exposure promotes tolerance. LEAP means Learning Early About Peanut Allergy; EAT means Enquiring About Tolerance.

 These trials informed the shift away from delaying common food allergens. Australian guidelines now recommend introduction at around 6 months, when the infant is developmentally ready, rather than delay.

cards.front: A right-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia is easily missed because the liver plugs the defect, so the film shows an apparently elevated hemidiaphragm rather than the [___] lucency seen on the left.
cards.context:
Right-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia is the one that gets missed, and the reason is mechanical.

The liver plugs the defect, so little or no bowel enters the chest and the bubbly lucency that makes the left-sided case obvious never appears.

The film may show only an apparently elevated right hemidiaphragm or a vague basal opacity, and presentation is correspondingly delayed.

cards.front: Arthritis (clinical diagnosis) = joint [___]/effusion alone, OR 2+ of tenderness, pain on movement, limited movement, increased warmth.
cards.context:
Arthritis is a clinical diagnosis. Objective joint swelling or effusion alone is enough to call it arthritis.

If there is no swelling/effusion, you need at least 2 (that is what '2+' means) of: tenderness, pain on movement, limited movement, increased warmth.

Two or more soft signs together separate true arthritis from arthralgia — joint pain with no inflammation. True arthritis triggers different workup — rheumatology referral, autoimmune screen.

cards.front: Once the femoral head has ossified after about 6 months, first-line imaging for suspected developmental dysplasia of the hip changes to [___].
cards.context: Ultrasound is preferred before 6 months while the hip is cartilaginous. Once the femoral head ossifies, plain radiography shows hip alignment and acetabular development better.

cards.front: Global developmental delay workup: chromosomal microarray, [___] X testing, thyroid function, metabolic screen; brain MRI if neurological signs.
cards.context:
Global developmental delay is delay in two or more domains. Start with chromosomal microarray, a separate Fragile X assay, thyroid function and history-directed metabolic testing.

Test hearing and vision in every child. Reserve brain MRI and neurology review for focal signs, dysmorphism, abnormal head size or regression.

Refer to a child-development service or general paediatrician, and begin early intervention while investigations proceed.

cards.front: A single palmar crease, a sandal gap or a preauricular pit have no consequence on their own — each is a [___] anomaly, not a malformation needing treatment.
cards.context:
Major malformations impair function or need treatment: for example, a cardiac defect, cleft palate or neural-tube defect. Minor anomalies such as a palmar crease, sandal gap or preauricular pit do not.

Majors drive immediate management; minors are diagnostic clues.

cards.front: A paediatric forearm fracture with one cortex broken and the opposite cortex bent is a [___] fracture.
cards.context:
A greenstick fracture is incomplete: one cortex breaks while the opposite cortex bends. A buckle fracture is a metaphyseal compression failure without a complete cortical break.

Name the pattern explicitly when describing a paediatric fracture, then add site and displacement.

cards.front: A paediatric inguinal hernia passes through a persistent embryological tract, so it is always [___] and never resolves spontaneously.
cards.context:
In girls the patent tract is the canal of Nuck, the female equivalent of the processus vaginalis.

As in boys, it is a persistent embryological passage rather than a weakness that develops, which is why a paediatric inguinal hernia is always indirect and never resolves on its own.

cards.front: In paediatric functional constipation, the commonest cause of treatment failure is stopping [___] too early; maintain for at least 3-6 months after regular stools.
cards.context:
Chronic constipation dilates the rectum and dulls the sensation of urge — disimpaction and a few weeks of regular stools doesn't reverse it. Stop laxatives early and the cycle restarts within days.

Maintain macrogol for ≥3-6 months after regular stools, then wean slowly over weeks. Combine with toileting routine after meals (gastrocolic reflex), reward for cooperation (not outcome).

cards.front: Pubic and axillary hair with acne in a young child who has no breast or testicular development and a normal growth velocity reflects premature [___], not true precocious puberty.
cards.context:
Adrenarche (adrenal androgens → pubic/axillary hair, acne, body odour) can appear before true puberty and drives most 'premature adrenarche' referrals.

It is NOT gonadarche: there is no breast development or testicular enlargement, growth velocity is normal and bone age is not advanced — which is how it is told apart from true (central) precocious puberty.

cards.front: Per ANZCOR, a choking child with an ineffective cough gets 5 back blows then 5 [___] thrusts — the same at any age; Australia does not use abdominal thrusts.
cards.context:
Conscious choking child: encourage coughing if effective. If the cough becomes ineffective, give 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts — the SAME at every age.

ANZCOR does not recommend abdominal thrusts at ANY age (intra-abdominal injury risk), unlike overseas (ERC/AHA) guidelines that switch to abdominal thrusts over 1 year. Repeat cycles.

If unconscious — start CPR; check the mouth for a visible foreign body before each breath, NO blind finger sweeps.

cards.front: Isotretinoin is highly effective for severe acne but is teratogenic — requires two forms of contraception in females; also monitor LFTs, lipids, and [___].
cards.context:
Isotretinoin is the most effective severe-acne treatment but is highly teratogenic (craniofacial, cardiac, CNS, thymic anomalies).

Also monitor LFTs, fasting lipids, and mood (possible suicidality link). Avoid alcohol, tetracyclines (additive ICP risk), and waxing (skin fragility). Standard course is 4-6 months to cumulative ~120-150 mg/kg.

cards.front: Pyloric stenosis: onset age [___] weeks; projectile non-bilious vomiting + hungry after; bloods show hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
cards.context:
Pyloric stenosis: hypertrophic pyloric muscle obstructs gastric outflow, onset 2-8 weeks. Triad: projectile non-bilious vomiting, HUNGRY after (distinguishes from gastro), palpable 'olive' epigastric mass.

Bloods: hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (HCl loss). Treat with rehydration + Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.

cards.front: [___] of the newborn is delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid; more common after caesarean delivery; resolves within 24-72 hours.
cards.context:
TTN is the commonest cause of respiratory distress in term/near-term infants in the first hours of life — delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid.

Clinical: tachypnoea 60-100/min, mild work of breathing, minimal O₂ need (FiO₂ <0.4). CXR shows 'wet lungs' — fluid in the horizontal fissure, perihilar streaking, hyperinflation.

Caesarean raises risk (no chest squeeze/catecholamine surge to absorb fluid). Self-limiting diagnosis of exclusion; trap is mistaking it for sepsis or RDS, so septic screen ± antibiotics until ruled out.

cards.front: Epiglottitis is classically caused by Haemophilus [___] type b — rare now due to vaccination; child is toxic, drooling, in tripod posture.
cards.context:
Hib epiglottitis was once common in 2-7 year olds but has been nearly eliminated by routine Hib vaccination. Now consider it in unvaccinated children, immigrants, and unusual organisms (Group A Strep, S. aureus).

Tripod posture (sitting forward with neck extended, mouth open) optimises airway patency in the face of supraglottic obstruction.

cards.front: Beyond leukaemia and CNS tumours, the childhood-characteristic cancers are the [___] (neuroblastoma, Wilms', retinoblastoma, hepatoblastoma); adult cancer is dominated by carcinomas.
cards.context:
Childhood cancer is dominated by leukaemia (~30%), CNS tumours (~20%), and solid tumours arising from persistent fetal tissue — neuroblastoma, nephroblastoma, retinoblastoma, hepatoblastoma.

Epithelial cancers of breast, bowel, lung, and prostate need decades of acquired mutations, so they dominate adult practice and are vanishingly rare in children.

cards.front: inspiratory stridor = upper airway; [___] wheeze = lower airway; biphasic stridor = fixed glottic/subglottic lesion; grunting = airspace pathology.
cards.context:
The phase of the noise localises the lesion.

Expiratory wheeze: intrathoracic small airways collapse as pressure rises — lower airway obstruction (asthma, bronchiolitis).

Biphasic stridor = fixed glottic/subglottic obstruction. Grunting = self-PEEP against airspace pathology (pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, RDS).

cards.front: Cerebral palsy: non-progressive motor disorder from developing-brain injury; prevalence 2 per 1000 live births; [___] is the most common motor type.
cards.context:
Cerebral palsy is a NON-PROGRESSIVE motor disorder caused by injury to the developing brain — the brain injury itself is fixed but motor manifestations may evolve as the child grows. Prevalence 2 per 1000 live births.

Classified by topography (hemiplegia, diplegia, quadriplegia) and motor type (spastic ~80%, dyskinetic, ataxic).

Risk factors: prematurity, low birthweight, perinatal asphyxia, neonatal encephalopathy.
